title: Behavioral Memory under Symmetry in One-Way Quantum Automata
abstract: Under compact symmetry, observable behavior reduces to an invariant operator algebra, but its dimension is not yet classical memory: some coordinates are dynamically frozen, some invisible to threshold tests, and some already classical. We develop an operator-algebraic theory that separates these effects through three filters. For one automaton, behavior is the Hilbert--Schmidt pairing between prefix-reachable states and suffix-observable effects, whose rank equals the real Hankel rank without controllability or observability assumptions. Maximizing this invariant over a symmetry-constrained dynamical class gives a structural capacity controlled by the symmetry commutant: its center stores isotypic populations frozen by reversible dynamics, its traceless multiplicity blocks carry movable noncommutative coordinates, dissipation removes the unary spectral loss inside those blocks, and covariant mobility releases relative populations subject to component conservation. Operational realization then determines which surviving coordinates force probabilistic states. For a fixed nontrivial invariant readout, full mobility gives an exact dichotomy in worst-case state cost: a commutative invariant algebra costs exactly its dimension, whereas a noncommutative multiplicity block raises the unrestricted cost by exactly one state. Thus noncommutativity has a one-state worst-case classical price. The known four-letter quadratic-plus-one law at trivial symmetry is the fully mobile endpoint of this principle. Schur--Weyl duality further shows that different preserved symmetries on the same tensor-power Hilbert space can change the worst memory scale from polynomial to exponential, while fixed-weight modules give an exact Catalan law at half filling, with structural capacity equal to the Catalan count minus its central-sector correction.
summary: This theoretical paper analyzes the memory capacity of one-way quantum automata under symmetry constraints using advanced operator algebra. It develops a framework that quantifies memory by analyzing the rank of associated Hankel matrices and decomposes the system's dynamics into components related to symmetry. The key finding is that noncommutativity imposes a quantifiable, one-state penalty on the worst-case computational cost.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop an operator-algebraic theory to characterize the 'behavioral memory' of one-way quantum automata when subjected to compact symmetry constraints.
main_result: It establishes a sharp dichotomy where noncommutativity in the invariant algebra raises the worst-case classical cost by exactly one state, and it relates memory capacity to structural properties like the commutant's center and multiplicity blocks.
method: The authors employ operator-algebraic techniques, defining behavior via the Hilbert-Schmidt pairing and analyzing the rank of the acceptance Hankel matrix, $ eta(A)$.
model_or_system: The model is the one-way quantum automaton, whose evolution and memory are captured by an acceptance function $f_A(w)$ and analyzed through its associated operator algebra.
key_observables: Behavioral Memory ($ eta(A)$), Operational Strict-Cutpoint Memory ($	ext{scPFA},_R(A, 	au)$), and the rank of the acceptance Hankel matrix.
important_parameters: The structure of the symmetry commutant, the dimension of the invariant algebra, and the state cost associated with commutativity vs. noncommutativity.
main_assumptions: The analysis focuses on the scope of strict-cutpoint language recognition by real PFAs, and the theory distinguishes between different comparison classes of quantum channels.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the memory measure using Hankel matrices, deriving an exact formula for the linear memory dimension via isotypic decomposition, and then analyzing the structural cost implications based on the algebraic properties (commutativity vs. noncommutativity) of the symmetry-constrained invariant algebra.
why_interesting: The rigorous connection drawn between algebraic structure (commutativity) and computational cost (state cost) provides a powerful, general framework for understanding resource limitations in quantum computation models.
